title: Al-Basir, the All-Seeing
tomorrow: why did the Prophet change a man's nickname, 'the judge'?

cards: Location sharing. One friend loves it: somebody always knows where I am. Another friend turned it off the week she got it, because it felt like a leash.
Same little dot on a map, two completely different feelings. Yesterday's question lands right there. If Allah is always seeing, is that a threat or a comfort?
Al-Basir, the All-Seeing. And the honest answer is that the Qur'an uses it both ways, so let both sides make their case.

teach.b: First side: being seen keeps you honest. In Surah al-Alaq, a man tries to stop a servant of God from praying, and the Qur'an asks him, in Pickthall's words: "Is he then unaware that Allah seeth?" That's a warning.
Some teachers of the inner life built a practice on it called muraqaba, watchfulness, holding in mind that you're seen so you act straight when no one else is around.
The best case for this side: people act differently when a camera is on, and this one never turns off. Second side: being seen is company.

teach.h: A COMFORT: I AM WITH YOU.
teach.b: Moses and Aaron are scared to face Pharaoh, and God tells them: "Fear not. Lo! I am with you twain, Hearing and Seeing." Nobody is being scolded there. Being seen is the reason to walk in.
The best case for this side: fear wears thin, but being seen by someone who's on your side gives you nerve. Now the line to tell a friend tonight.
In the hadith of Jibril, the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, defines ihsan, doing things beautifully, like this: worship Allah as though you see Him, and if you do not see Him, He sees you.
Both sides are in that sentence. Which one you hear first may change with the week.

how: Muslims speak of ihsan, worshiping as though you see Allah, knowing He sees you; some practice muraqaba, a deliberate watchfulness of the heart, as part of daily devotion.

o: the All-Seeing, a warning and a comfort
the one who sees only in the mosque
the one who sees only the good you do

games.q: two sides, one Name — tap the pairs.
p: a warning: is he unaware Allah sees?
comfort: I am with you, seeing
worship as though you see Him

s: in the Qur'an, 'Allah sees you' is only ever a threat
to Moses and Aaron it's comfort: "I am with you twain, Hearing and Seeing."
the hadith of Jibril defines ihsan in terms of seeing
worship as though you see Him; and if you don't see Him, He sees you.

games.q: in your study circle, one friend says God watching should keep you scared straight. another says it should feel like company. you're asked to sum up fairly. which is fairest to the Qur'an?
o: only the first; comfort is a soft modern spin.
both are in the text: a warning in al-Alaq, comfort to Moses and Aaron.
only the second; the warning verses were for one man long ago.
games.why: the Qur'an uses Allah's seeing both ways, and the hadith of Jibril holds both in one sentence. neither friend has to lose.

practice: Do one small thing right now that nobody will ever notice: straighten the shoes by the door, wipe a counter, put one stray thing back where it lives. No photo, no mention.
Then sit for the two minutes and let yourself be seen doing nothing at all.

wordCard.voice: Al-Basir. The All-Seeing: a warning to the man who blocks a prayer, and company for two brothers walking in to face Pharaoh.

orig.note: Arabic: the All-Seeing. often paired in the Qur'an with As-Sami', the All-Hearing.

carryVoice: Carry this: seen, at the door and on the hard walk in, whichever you need today. That's day fifteen-oh-one.
